Shuffle sequences keeping their k-mer counts

Source: R/sequence-shuffle.R
gseq.shuffle.Rd

Draws random sequences with exactly the same k-mer counts as the input sequences - the dinucleotide counts with the default k = 2 - for use as a composition-matched background, e.g. in motif enrichment.

Usage

gseq.shuffle(seqs, k = 2L, n = 1L, seed = NULL)

Arguments

seqs

a character vector of DNA sequences (NA gives NA), or an intervals data frame, whose sequences are read with gseq.extract (strand-aware).

k

the k-mer length whose counts are kept, 1 to 32. Default 2 (dinucleotides).

n

the number of shuffles of each sequence.

seed

a whole number (|seed| <= 2^53) seeding the shuffle, or NULL to draw one from R's random number generator.

Value

With n = 1, a character vector like seqs (names kept). With n > 1, a character matrix with a row per sequence and a column per shuffle.

Details

Each shuffle is drawn uniformly at random from all the sequences that keep the k-mer counts and the first k-1 bases. The construction is the Eulerian-path one of Altschul & Erickson (1985) and Kandel et al. (1996), as in uShuffle (Jiang et al. 2008): the (k-1)-mers are the vertices of a graph whose edges are the k-mers of the sequence, a uniformly random spanning tree of "last exits" is drawn with Wilson's algorithm, and the remaining edges out of each vertex are put in a random order. k = 1 is a plain random permutation of the bases. Because the k-mers form a path through the (k-1)-mers, the last k-1 bases are kept too.

Only A, C, G and T (in either case) are shuffled. Any other character - N, an IUPAC code, a gap - stays at its position and splits the sequence into segments, each shuffled on its own; the k-mers that touch such a character are therefore unchanged, and the k-mer counts of the whole sequence, N-containing k-mers included, are kept. Shuffling the N's into the sequence instead would scatter assembly gaps across it. Bases are compared ignoring case and every position keeps its case, so a soft-masked stretch stays lowercase at the same coordinates (with new bases in it); toupper() the input first to ignore case altogether. A segment of k bases or fewer has only one arrangement and is returned as is.

The random numbers come from misha's own generator (xoshiro256**), not from R's: with a seed the result does not depend on, and does not change, R's random number state, and is the same on every platform and the same as PyMisha's gseq_shuffle for the same seed. Without a seed one is drawn from R's generator, so set.seed() makes the call reproducible (but the sequences then differ from PyMisha's, whose generator differs). Each input sequence gets its own random stream, derived from the seed and its position in seqs, so its shuffles do not depend on the sequences that come after it.

References

Altschul SF, Erickson BW (1985). Significance of nucleotide sequence alignments: a method for random sequence permutation that preserves dinucleotide and codon usage. Mol Biol Evol 2(6):526-538.

Kandel D, Matias Y, Unger R, Winkler P (1996). Shuffling biological sequences. Discrete Applied Mathematics 71:171-185.

Jiang M, Anderson J, Gillespie J, Mayne M (2008). uShuffle: a useful tool for shuffling biological sequences while preserving the k-let counts. BMC Bioinformatics 9:192.

See also

gseq.kmer, gseq.kmer.dist, gsynth.sample for sampling from a Markov model, which keeps the expected composition rather than the exact counts.

Examples

seqs <- c(a = "ACGTTGCAACGTAGCTAGCTTTACG", b = "ccgNNacgtacgtTTGACG")
gseq.shuffle(seqs, seed = 1)
#>                           a                           b 
#> "AACTAGTTTGCGCACGTTAGCTACG"       "ccgNNacgacgtgTTTACG" 

# three shuffles of each sequence, keeping trinucleotide counts
gseq.shuffle(seqs, k = 3, n = 3, seed = 1)
#>   [,1]                        [,2]                       
#> a "ACGTAGCTAGCTTGCAACGTTTACG" "ACGTTTGCAACGTAGCTAGCTTACG"
#> b "ccgNNacgtacgtTTGACG"       "ccgNNacgtacgtTTGACG"      
#>   [,3]                       
#> a "ACGTTAGCTACGTAGCTTTGCAACG"
#> b "ccgNNacgtttgaCGTACG"      

# the dinucleotide counts are unchanged
sh <- gseq.shuffle(seqs[["a"]], seed = 7)
identical(
    table(substring(sh, 1:24, 2:25)),
    table(substring(seqs[["a"]], 1:24, 2:25))
)
#> [1] TRUE
